title: How cutting emissions is future-proofing industries beyond the ‘green premium’
gist: A Radio Davos podcast transcript (one continuous episode, not a hub page) built around three interviews from a First Movers Coalition event: LanzaTech's CEO on carbon-recycling economics, Oberon Fuels' CEO on renewable DME, and a Khosla Ventures partner on cost-driven climate investing — all converging on the idea that the 'green premium' is a temporary deployment problem, now increasingly reframed as a 'security premium' tied to supply-chain resilience and AI-era energy demand.

themes.theme: Green premium as a bridge, not a destination

insights.claim: The green premium is a temporary bridge that gets eliminated through deployment scale, not a permanent cost that green technologies must carry forever — as seen historically with solar, wind and cellphones.
insights.speaker: Jennifer Holmgren
insights.so_what: Investors should value clean-tech bets on their cost-curve trajectory (deployment volume driving cost down) rather than assuming a permanent price gap needs subsidy forever.
insights.quote: The more you build, the cheaper it gets, the cheaper it gets, the more you build.
insights.locator: To get rid of a green premium, it's just a deployment story

insights.claim: There is effectively no green premium left for renewable electricity ('green electrons') from solar and wind because deployment drove costs to parity with fossil generation, and the same cost-curve dynamic is expected to eventually apply to 'green molecules' like ethanol and sustainable aviation fuel.
insights.speaker: Jennifer Holmgren
insights.so_what: Signals that green fuels/molecules are several deployment cycles behind renewable power on the cost curve — an early-stage window for investors betting on eventual parity.
insights.locator: There is no real green premium for green electrons anymore, is there?

insights.claim: Financing green fuel plants fails when treated like electron power-purchase agreements: molecules trade on volatile spot markets, so a 10-year fixed-price offtake on a higher-cost molecule (e.g. $5,000/tonne sustainable aviation fuel versus $2,000/tonne conventional jet fuel) is too large and risky a commitment for buyers, unlike the small per-kilowatt-hour commitments that financed solar and wind.
insights.speaker: Jennifer Holmgren
insights.so_what: Explains why molecule-based decarbonization (SAF, green ethanol, green hydrogen) is financing-constrained in a way electron-based renewables were not — a structural bottleneck financiers and policymakers need new instruments to solve.
insights.quote: Do they really want to commit to pay $5,000 a tonne when conventional jet fuel is $2,000, a tonne?
insights.locator: Why could you not get those long-term contracts now?

insights.claim: Financing a new green-fuel plant currently takes about five years and needs to shrink to roughly two years for the industry to build enough plants to erode the green premium.
insights.speaker: Jennifer Holmgren
insights.so_what: Financing-cycle speed, not just technology cost, is a binding constraint on how fast green-molecule industries can scale — a metric to track for capacity build-out timing.
insights.quote: we've got to stop taking five years to finance the plant. We need to take two years.
insights.locator: Where do you see your industry in five years time or in 10 years time?

insights.claim: Corporate buyer conversations about green products have shifted from asking how a product helps decarbonize to asking what it costs, when it can be delivered, and how it scales — a sign the sustainability sector is maturing into an ordinary commercial market rather than a purely values-driven one.
insights.speaker: Rebecca Boudreaux
insights.so_what: A maturing buyer conversation (cost/delivery/scale over pure ESG narrative) is a leading indicator that a green-tech category is nearing commercial viability, useful for timing investment or partnership entry.
insights.quote: what does it cost, when can I get it, and how does it scale?
insights.locator: You do see that, and there's a shift in the conversation

themes.theme: First Movers Coalition: pooling demand in hard-to-abate sectors

insights.claim: The First Movers Coalition, launched around 2021, works by pooling corporate offtake demand signals across seven hard-to-abate sectors — aluminium, steel, cement/concrete, shipping, trucking, aviation and carbon dioxide removal — to give investors and project developers confidence that unscaled clean technologies will have buyers by 2030.
insights.speaker: Noam Boussidan
insights.so_what: The Coalition is effectively a demand-aggregation mechanism investors can watch as a proxy for de-risking specific hard-to-abate technology bets.
insights.locator: The First Movers Coalition, FMC by its short name, is a collective effort

insights.claim: The First Movers Coalition has shifted its internal focus over five years from setting ambition and commitments to actually delivering on them, reflecting a broader maturation stage for corporate climate initiatives.
insights.speaker: Noam Boussidan
insights.so_what: Investors should now judge FMC-aligned companies on delivery/execution metrics rather than pledges, since the coalition itself says the pledge phase is over.
insights.locator: FMC Day, five years later, takes you into a place whereby those commitments were made

insights.claim: Despite political swings against climate action and 'green hushing' (companies quietly downplaying their green efforts publicly), First Movers Coalition leadership and its member-company representatives say the underlying corporate direction of travel toward decarbonization commitments has not reversed.
insights.speaker: Noam Boussidan
insights.so_what: Pushes back against a narrative of corporate ESG retreat — worth stress-testing against actual capex/offtake data rather than public messaging, since messaging itself is what's said to be muted.
insights.locator: your observation that the pendulum swings is absolutely a right one

insights.claim: First-mover buyers like airline group IAG and utility Vattenfall have absorbed higher costs to commit to green fuel offtake, but their volume alone is insufficient to reach the scale needed, meaning 'fast follower' buyers must now join to create enough demand.
insights.speaker: Jennifer Holmgren
insights.so_what: Tracking which large buyers move from pilot/first-mover deals to repeat, larger offtake commitments is a concrete signal of when a green-fuel category is inflecting toward scale.
insights.locator: We work with IAG, and they're willing to do that

insights.claim: LanzaTech captures CO2 or CO industrial off-gases directly at emission sites (e.g. steel mills) and uses bacterial fermentation — completed in seconds rather than the long timescales of sugar fermentation — to convert them directly into ethanol, functioning more like a refinery than a traditional fermenter.
insights.speaker: Jennifer Holmgren
insights.so_what: The speed and site-integration of the process is what makes carbon-recycling economically viable at industrial scale rather than a lab curiosity.
insights.locator: It looks like a biorefinery connected to the steel mill

insights.claim: LanzaTech operates four commercial plants in China converting steel and ferroalloy off-gases into ethanol, plus a plant with ArcelorMittal in Ghent, Belgium — proof the carbon-recycling process already runs at commercial scale, not just pilot scale.
insights.speaker: Jennifer Holmgren
insights.so_what: Concrete operating asset count/geography for tracking LanzaTech's commercial footprint and expansion into the West.
insights.locator: we have four commercial plants operating in China

insights.claim: LanzaTech's China joint venture went public on the Hong Kong exchange and its plants earn 20–30% operating margins selling ethanol into the ordinary road-transport fuel market — not through carbon credits or a special green premium — demonstrating that carbon-recycled ethanol is commercially profitable on its own merits.
insights.speaker: Jennifer Holmgren
insights.so_what: A rare case of a decarbonization technology already generating strong margins without subsidy dependence — a template for what 'beyond the green premium' looks like in practice.
insights.quote: they have 20 to 30% margins in their operating plants
insights.locator: Our JV in China just went public on the Hong Kong exchange

insights.claim: LanzaTech converts its recycled ethanol into sustainable aviation fuel through LanzaJet (47% owned by LanzaTech), which operates a commercial-scale plant in Georgia, US producing 10 million gallons per year.
insights.speaker: Jennifer Holmgren
insights.so_what: A concrete capacity figure and ownership structure for anyone evaluating LanzaJet/LanzaTech's SAF supply chain economics.
insights.locator: a large commercial plant converting ethanol to sustainable aviation fuel in Georgia at a 10 million gallon a year scale

insights.claim: Ethanol can substitute for methanol in marine engines while carrying about 40% more energy density, letting ships carry more cargo per voyage for the same fuel volume — a 'drop-in' fuel advantage that avoids new engine infrastructure.
insights.speaker: Jennifer Holmgren
insights.so_what: A specific technical edge (energy density) that could tilt shipping-fuel buyer preference toward ethanol over methanol independent of any carbon argument.
insights.quote: it has 40% more energy density
insights.locator: Ethanol can go into marine fuel

insights.claim: Global fossil carbon consumption is roughly 100 million barrels a day, which is why LanzaTech deliberately built its process around a broad feedstock pool — industrial waste, gasified municipal solid waste, and agricultural/forestry waste — rather than a single input, arguing that only a similarly massive and diverse feedstock base can scale to matter.
insights.speaker: Jennifer Holmgren
insights.so_what: Feedstock diversity/scale is a screening criterion investors can use to judge whether a carbon-recycling technology can ever reach meaningful global volume.
insights.quote: the world uses 100 million barrels a day of fossil carbon
insights.locator: finally a technology approach that can scale the way the refining industry scaled

insights.claim: Feedstock-specific policy design creates barriers for new carbon-recycling technologies — LanzaTech's first industrial carbon-recycling scheme did not qualify for any existing incentive category — so Holmgren argues policy should be made technology-neutral instead.
insights.speaker: Jennifer Holmgren
insights.so_what: A concrete policy-design flaw investors and policymakers should watch for when assessing subsidy/regulatory regimes for new decarbonization technologies.
insights.quote: The first time we built our first industrial carbon recycling scheme, we didn't qualify for anything.
insights.locator: you need technology-neutral standards

insights.claim: China's advantage in fast building and fast prototyping ('fast fail, fast build') — illustrated by its move to sodium-based batteries while the West stayed focused on lithium — is why LanzaTech's first commercial deployments launched there, and Holmgren pushes back on the idea that China only duplicates rather than innovates.
insights.speaker: Jennifer Holmgren
insights.so_what: Challenges a common Western investor assumption (China = copying, not inventing) that could mean underpricing Chinese-originated clean-tech IP and manufacturing capability.
insights.quote: I think the West has fallen into a trap of thinking that China doesn't innovate. I disagree with that.
insights.locator: China builds things very, very fast and speed matters

themes.theme: Oberon Fuels: renewable DME and the HFC replacement opportunity

insights.claim: Oberon Fuels converts waste methanol byproduct from tree pulp/paper processing, plus other organic waste streams, into renewable dimethyl ether (DME), which is sold as a propane-blend transport fuel and increasingly as an aerosol propellant.
insights.speaker: Rebecca Boudreaux
insights.so_what: Defines the specific waste-to-chemical pathway and dual end markets (fuel and specialty chemicals) an investor would need to model for this company.
insights.locator: Oberon Fuels converts various waste streams to renewable fuels and chemicals

insights.claim: Renewable DME is positioned to replace hydrofluorocarbon (HFC) aerosol propellants and is already cost-competitive with HFCs today — a case where the green alternative carries no price premium at all, unlike most other green-fuel substitutions discussed in this episode.
insights.speaker: Rebecca Boudreaux
insights.so_what: A concrete counterexample to the 'green premium' framing worth flagging: a decarbonization product that is already price-competitive without subsidy, in a market (aerosols) facing regulatory phase-down of HFCs.
insights.quote: it's actually cost competitive with hydrofluorocarbons
insights.locator: the hydrofluorocarbons we are replacing are quite expensive

insights.claim: Getting a large corporation to adopt a new green input requires an internal champion who can mobilize procurement, safety and R&D teams simultaneously, since existing testing protocols and supply processes built for the fossil-based version often don't transfer to the new renewable product — illustrated by Oberon's selection into L'Oreal's L'Accelerator program (13 of roughly 1,000 applicants globally), led by L'Oreal's Chief Corporate Responsibility Officer.
insights.speaker: Rebecca Boudreaux
insights.so_what: A practical filter for evaluating whether a green-materials startup's corporate partnerships will actually convert to volume: look for a named internal champion and cross-functional buy-in, not just a signed MOU.
insights.locator: they created the L'Accelerator

insights.claim: Oberon Fuels' commercial partners span heavy trucking fuel (Volvo Trucks, Mack Trucks, Ford, Suburban Propane) and specialty consumer chemicals (Aeropress, the largest U.S. aerosol propellant distributor, and L'Oreal), showing renewable DME's addressable market spans both transport fuel and specialty chemicals.
insights.speaker: Rebecca Boudreaux
insights.so_what: Diversified end-market exposure (fuel blending plus consumer specialty chemicals) reduces Oberon's dependence on any single regulatory or subsidy regime.
insights.locator: We've had partnerships with Volvo trucks, Mack Trucks, Ford, Suburban Propane

themes.theme: Khosla Ventures: techno-economics over subsidy, and betting on future baseload power

insights.claim: Khosla Ventures deliberately excluded IRA subsidies, green premiums and tax credits from its climate investment memos during the 'climate 2.0' hype cycle, screening deals purely on capex/opex cost trajectory ('techno-economics') toward beating fossil-fuel commodity prices outright.
insights.speaker: Rajesh Swaminathan
insights.so_what: A concrete, replicable investment screen investors can apply to climate-tech deal flow: does the technology have a credible path to being cheaper than fossil fuels without subsidy?
insights.quote: none of our investment memos captured anything about IRA, green premium, tax credits, all of that, and intentionally so
insights.locator: The biggest focus we have is what we call as the 'Chindia' price

insights.claim: Khosla Ventures was the first institutional investor in OpenAI and invested in Commonwealth Fusion Systems the same month in 2018, treating both as future trillion-dollar companies on different timelines — reflecting a generalist strategy of backing the highest-impact bets regardless of sector.
insights.speaker: Rajesh Swaminathan
insights.so_what: Signals Khosla views frontier climate infrastructure (fusion) as being on the same order of magnitude of potential outcome as OpenAI-scale AI bets, worth benchmarking against.
insights.quote: we think both are trillion dollar companies, just the timing might be a little bit apart
insights.locator: We invested in Commonwealth Fusion in 2018. Around the same month, we invested in OpenAI

insights.claim: Khosla views nuclear fusion and geothermal as the only two power sources capable of true 24/7 baseload generation (solar and batteries cannot match consistent baseload), and expects super-hot-rock geothermal to reach commercialization before fusion, with both aimed at delivering under 5 cents per kilowatt-hour of baseload power.
insights.speaker: Rajesh Swaminathan
insights.so_what: A specific cost target (sub-5-cents/kWh) and relative timeline (geothermal before fusion) investors can use to benchmark progress in both sectors.
insights.quote: less than five cents a kilowatt hour 24-7 base load power
insights.locator: Geothermal is another one

insights.claim: Khosla's steel bet, Hertha, beat out rival approaches like molten electrolysis and electrochemistry-based steelmaking by using a single-step, lower-equipment-count process than conventional coke/blast-furnace/basic-oxygen-furnace plants, reaching one tonne/day (300 tonnes/year) output on just $15 million in capital, versus rivals that spent $200-300 million without reaching that output level.
insights.speaker: Rajesh Swaminathan
insights.so_what: A stark capital-efficiency benchmark ($15M vs $200-300M for similar output) that investors can use to compare steel-decarbonization startups' capital discipline.
insights.quote: with just 15 million dollars, they were able to get to one tonne per day, 300 tonnes per year
insights.locator: we saw a company called Hertha

insights.claim: Khosla's hydrogen bet, Verdagy, succeeded by pivoting from a chlor-alkali process (making ethylene dichloride for PVC) rather than starting as a dedicated electrolyzer company, letting it reach $3/kg green hydrogen cost without any IRA subsidy — undercutting PEM and alkaline electrolyzer peers stuck at $7-9/kg even with a $3/kg IRA subsidy — and it is now building a Gigafactory targeting $2/kg within 2-2.5 years, already cheaper than Chinese electrolyzers.
insights.speaker: Rajesh Swaminathan
insights.so_what: A concrete, subsidy-independent cost benchmark ($3/kg now, $2/kg target) for evaluating green hydrogen competitiveness against both fossil ('grey') hydrogen and Chinese electrolyzer suppliers.
insights.quote: five years later, today, they are actually at $3 a kilogramme without any kind of IRA green premium needed
insights.locator: Instead, we bet on a company called Verdagy

insights.claim: Green hydrogen priced at $2-3/kg is a particularly large opportunity for import-dependent countries like India, where expensive imported natural gas makes even fossil-derived 'grey' hydrogen costly, unlike the U.S. which produces natural gas domestically.
insights.speaker: Rajesh Swaminathan
insights.so_what: Identifies India specifically as a differentiated green-hydrogen demand market driven by domestic gas economics rather than climate policy alone.
insights.locator: There is a strong demand for countries like India to go after hydrogen

insights.claim: Khosla advises founders to build climate-tech companies assuming regulatory/subsidy support will not be there, treating any subsidy that does materialize as pure upside margin rather than a foundational assumption.
insights.speaker: Rajesh Swaminathan
insights.so_what: A durable underwriting principle for evaluating climate-tech business models against policy risk (e.g. subsidy repeal).
insights.quote: you can't build a company assuming the regulatory support will be there
insights.locator: I think regulatory makes a difference

insights.claim: Swaminathan frames climate technology deployment as needing large incumbent companies to partner with disruptive startups rather than compete against them, describing it as a 'David and Goliath' (collaborative) story rather than a 'David versus Goliath' (adversarial) one.
insights.speaker: Rajesh Swaminathan
insights.so_what: Suggests investors should look for incumbent-startup partnership structures (not pure startup disruption plays) as the likelier path to commercial scale in hard-to-abate industries.
insights.quote: I look at climate as really not a David versus Goliath story, it's a David and Goliath story.
insights.locator: Some of the large companies need to partner with these startups

insights.claim: Swaminathan warns that the West has repeatedly invented core clean-energy technology — semiconductors, solar, and batteries — only to lose the manufacturing scale-up to China, and argues the same risk now applies to cement, steel, geothermal and fusion, framing clean-tech manufacturing as a geopolitical wealth-and-jobs issue rather than only an environmental one.
insights.speaker: Rajesh Swaminathan
insights.so_what: Frames Western clean-tech manufacturing policy support as a competitiveness/national-security issue, useful context for evaluating industrial-policy tailwinds (e.g. reshoring incentives) for steel/cement/geothermal startups.
insights.quote: We cannot afford to lose that, both from a geopolitical perspective, as well as building competency in these countries
insights.locator: I was in Bell Labs. I have been in semiconductor industry

insights.claim: Khosla is 'very bullish' on critical minerals, specifically the intersection with AI: using AI to speed up discovery of new mineral deposits and to make mining/extraction faster and cheaper.
insights.speaker: Rajesh Swaminathan
insights.so_what: Flags critical-minerals-plus-AI as a specific sector Khosla is actively deploying capital into — a theme to watch for follow-on deals.
insights.locator: I think critical minerals is a big one

themes.theme: Green premium reframed as a security premium

insights.claim: First Movers Coalition observed a shift in how buyers justify paying more for alternative technologies: from a pure 'green premium' framed around carbon benefits to a 'security premium' framed around supply diversification and resilience, sharpened by 2026's Strait of Hormuz disruption, which hindered roughly 20% of global oil and gas flows.
insights.speaker: Noam Boussidan
insights.so_what: A reframing that broadens the investment case for alternative fuels/materials beyond ESG into energy-security policy, potentially unlocking budget and political support that pure climate framing could not.
insights.quote: 20% of the global oil and gas flows are kind of hindered
insights.locator: the Strait of Hormuz is being blocked

insights.claim: The 'security premium' framing gives corporate champions a stronger case to convince CFOs and CEOs to invest in alternative technologies, because it bundles supply-chain resilience and energy diversification benefits on top of carbon reduction, broadening the investment rationale beyond pure ESG.
insights.speaker: Noam Boussidan
insights.so_what: Suggests deal teams pitching alternative-fuel or materials investments should emphasize security/resilience benefits alongside carbon metrics to win board approval in the current political climate.
insights.locator: that's significant shift. Has been happening, we've witnessed it

insights.claim: Holmgren frames LanzaTech's use of local waste feedstocks as inherently supporting energy security, and separately calls for the industry to pursue broader 'energy diversification' since molecule and electron supply chains have relied too heavily on the same limited set of resources.
insights.speaker: Jennifer Holmgren
insights.so_what: Positions local-feedstock carbon-recycling technology as a hedge against geopolitical supply disruption, not just a climate play.
insights.quote: We have spent way too much time with molecules and with electrons coming from the same exact resources.
insights.locator: I think energy security is quite important

themes.theme: AI's energy demand is reshaping the clean-power investment case

insights.claim: Swaminathan predicts the ultimate winner of the AI race will be determined less by who has the best language model and more by who has the best access to compute and energy, making baseload clean power a strategic input to AI competitiveness rather than a side issue.
insights.speaker: Rajesh Swaminathan
insights.so_what: Reframes clean baseload power (geothermal, fusion, even domestic oil/gas) as AI infrastructure, meaning capital allocators evaluating AI exposure should also be evaluating power-generation bets.
insights.quote: the country that has the best language model may not be the winner. The winner will be somebody who has right access to compute and energy.
insights.locator: Because as you think about AI

insights.claim: Khosla explicitly ties its geothermal and nuclear fusion investment thesis to powering AI data centers, arguing that whether the same 24/7 baseload capacity is called 'geothermal,' 'drill baby drill,' or clean power for AI, the underlying goal is the same: providing secure, low-cost, always-on electricity that the AI buildout requires.
insights.speaker: Rajesh Swaminathan
insights.so_what: Suggests investors can treat baseload clean-power startups as a levered bet on AI infrastructure demand, independent of their climate framing, and that political messaging around them (climate vs. energy security vs. 'drill baby drill') may not affect the underlying investment thesis.
insights.quote: It doesn't matter what you call it. At the end of the day, this is really leveraging the oil and gas capability with the geothermal capability that exists to provide clean power for AI and data centre world
insights.locator: Even in the US, if you look at it, I can call it as geothermal
